title: Fed Chair Warsh Signals Rate Hikes Possible as Inflation Stays Elevated
excerpt: In his debut Jackson Hole speech, Kevin Warsh said the Fed will 'have work to do' if inflation does not return to target, sending markets to price in 55 percent odds of a September rate hike.
body:
• Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the central bank will "have work to do" if policymakers lack confidence that inflation is returning to the 2 percent target
  • The PCE price index remained at 3.7 percent annually as of July, with Warsh calling progress over the past two years "modest"
  • Markets now price in roughly 55 percent odds of a 25 basis point rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting, up from about 35 percent before the speech
  • The S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell while the dollar rose to a session high following Warsh's hawkish remarks

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Friday delivered his clearest signal yet that interest rate hikes may be on the horizon, telling central bankers at the Jackson Hole symposium that the Fed will "have work to do" if it cannot gain confidence that inflation is returning to its 2 percent target.

The remarks, in Warsh's debut speech at the annual gathering in Wyoming, marked a sharp departure from the ambiguity that characterized his first two press conferences and sent markets scrambling to reprice the odds of a rate increase at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting.

Inflation Progress Called 'Modest'

"Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do," Warsh said. "That's our job ... our mandate ... and our charge to keep."

The Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, remained at 3.7 percent on an annual basis as of July — well above the central bank's 2 percent target and stubbornly elevated after more than five years above that level.

"Progress over the past two years has been modest," Warsh said, adding that recent data "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved." He noted that about half of the items in the PCE basket are increasing at more than a 3 percent annual rate, below the levels seen during the COVID-era inflation surge but above pre-pandemic norms.

Markets React to Hawkish Tone

Financial markets moved swiftly. Rate futures jumped to price in roughly a 55 percent chance of a 25 basis point rate hike at the September meeting, up from about 35 percent before the speech, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool and Reuters. The dollar rose to a session high, with the dollar index climbing 0.35 percent to 99.46.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq ended lower as investors turned cautious. Two-year Treasury yields moved sharply higher, reflecting growing conviction that tighter monetary policy is on the table.

"We're moving up on six years where we've been above target. You can't keep saying this is our job and then not act. Actions speak way louder than words."

— Patrick Harker, Former Philadelphia Fed President

A 'Quieter Fed' Speaks Up

Warsh, who replaced Jerome Powell on May 22, had previously frustrated markets by refusing to share his economic views or provide what analysts call "forward guidance" about future policy decisions. In a July press conference following the Fed's decision to hold rates steady in the 3.50 to 3.75 percent range, he gave away little about his thinking.

Friday's speech changed that calculus. While Warsh still maintained that "a quieter Fed, more purposeful in its communications, is better able to meet its objectives," he acknowledged that "short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate" and that credit and loan markets are "showing few signs of policy restraint."

Three policymakers dissented from the July decision to hold rates unchanged, and key unemployment, job growth, and consumer inflation data for August will be released early next month ahead of the September meeting.

Capital Economics analysts said the speech "delivered a far clearer — and hawkish — message than his last press conference appearance," adding that it "leaves the door open to a hike earlier than our current forecast of December, if the forthcoming price data are firm."

"We were encouraged by Warsh's speech. But talk is cheap."

— Aditya Bhave, Head of US Economics Research, Bank of America

Bank of America said the onus is now on Warsh to deliver a rate hike in September unless August jobs and inflation data come in very soft, warning that he would "probably lose credibility" otherwise.

Much of Warsh's 16-page address also touched on longer-term issues, including the role of artificial intelligence in the economy. He said recommendations from five task forces he established earlier in his tenure "will come later and have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture."
